notes: Oracle's Internet-native EBS 11i architecture gave temporary Internet-era advantage; SAP R/3 initially slower to Internet-enable; by 2003 SAP mySAP recovered

metric_value: Oracle presented softer customer-facing posture at AppsWorld 2002 — Ellison's 'kinder gentler' pivot toward applications customers
notes: Katherine Jones Aberdeen 2002 (14 obs): Oracle acknowledged applications customer pain; Ellison personally apologized for EBS 11i upgrade difficulties; major tone shift from aggressive 1990s posture

metric_value: Oracle shifted Applications strategy from module-centric to business-process-flow-centric 2003
notes: Katherine Jones Aberdeen 2003 (9 obs): Oracle adopted industry process frameworks; convergence with SAP's process orientation; precursor to Oracle Fusion process model

metric_value: Oracle Fusion Applications launched 2011 as next-generation cloud-native replacement for E-Business Suite and PeopleSoft
notes: Fusion Applications built on SOA/BPEL architecture; cloud delivery from 2012; Oracle Cloud ERP/HCM now primary growth vehicle; EBS and PeopleSoft maintained in extended support

metric_value: ~10 observations 2003–2005 on hostile takeover
notes: THREAD-7: PeopleSoft Hostile Acquisition. Oracle's 18-month hostile bid for PeopleSoft (2003–2004) was the defining enterprise software M&A event of the era; acquisition completed January 2005

metric_value: Oracle hostile bid for PeopleSoft rationalized as HCM capability acquisition + elimination of primary applications competitor
notes: Aberdeen 2003 (5 obs — Alschuler/Minahan): Oracle bid $16.30/share June 2003; PeopleSoft defended with poison pill; bid eventually raised to $26.50; 18-month contest

metric_value: PeopleSoft customers face significant disruption risk regardless of bid outcome — must plan for both scenarios
notes: Aberdeen 2003 advised PeopleSoft customers not to wait for bid resolution; evaluate hybrid scenarios; Oracle committed to 10-year PeopleSoft product support post-acquisition

metric_value: Oracle acquired PeopleSoft January 2005 for $10.3B after 18-month hostile contest; DOJ antitrust challenge failed
notes: Oracle paid $26.50/share; PeopleSoft board capitulated December 2004; Oracle immediately acquired Siebel 2006; acquisition thesis confirmed — hostile bids succeed in mature enterprise software

metric_value: PeopleSoft HCM and JD Edwards still actively deployed in 2026 — 21 years post-acquisition
notes: Oracle maintained PeopleSoft HCM and JDE product lines under extended support; large installed bases refused migration to Fusion; Oracle sold both migration path and continued maintenance

metric_value: ~60 observations 1997–2010 tracking Oracle8 through 10g
notes: THREAD-8: Oracle Database Evolution (Oracle8 through 10g). The core technology arc from object-relational to Internet-era to grid computing — the most densely observed Oracle technology thread

metric_value: Oracle8 introduced object-relational extensions — Oracle's answer to the object database challenge
notes: Kastner 1997 (20 obs): Oracle8 added object types / nested tables / object views; positioned as 'database for network computing'; Java stored procedures via Oracle8i (1999)

metric_value: Oracle8 positioned as the data tier of NCA — Java cartridges in the app server; Oracle8 as the persistence layer
notes: Kastner 1997: Oracle8 designed as the data backbone of the NCA stack; InterOffice as the groupware layer; Developer/2000 as the tooling layer — coherent but never fully realized as a platform

metric_value: Oracle9i Real Application Clusters provided active-active shared-disk high availability — technically superior to prior failover models
notes: Dorin Aberdeen 2001: Oracle9i RAC on Compaq Tru64 reduced HA costs vs. traditional standby; RAC became the dominant Oracle high-availability architecture

metric_value: Oracle 10g introduced Grid Computing branding — Oracle's reframing of multi-server architectures as 'utility computing grid'
notes: Kastner IT Themes 2003: Oracle 10g positioned database as grid resource; anti-Itanium / anti-big-iron messaging; aligned with Dell partnership on commodity x86

metric_value: Oracle Database maintained enterprise RDBMS market leadership continuously from Oracle7 (1992) through Oracle 23ai (2024)
notes: No version transition (7→8→8i→9i→10g→11g→12c→18c→19c→21c→23ai) produced a competitor displacement event; Oracle's database franchise is the most durable technology asset in the Kastner archive

metric_value: ~25 observations 1993–2026 on Larry Ellison as strategic actor
notes: THREAD-9: Larry Ellison Leadership and Competitive Style. Ellison is the archive's most-quoted executive after Lou Gerstner; his competitive posture defined Oracle's market behavior for four decades

metric_value: Larry Ellison adopted publicly softer posture toward Oracle Applications customers at AppsWorld 2002
notes: Katherine Jones Aberdeen 2002 (11 obs): 'A Kinder
collection: Gentler Larry Ellison' — Oracle acknowledged EBS 11i upgrade pain; Ellison personally engaged with user community; significant departure from 1990s combative style

metric_value: Larry Ellison predicted in 1995 that the PC was dead and would be replaced by the Network Computer within five years
notes: Ellison's PC-death prediction (1995–1996) was the most visible technology prediction refuted in the Oracle archive; PCs survived; Ellison's NC concept partly vindicated by iPad/Chromebook 15+ years later

metric_value: PC market continued to grow through 2010; NC devices failed commercially; Ellison prediction refuted on timeline and mechanism
notes: PC shipments grew from ~80M/year (1996) to ~350M/year (2010); NC device market never materialized; prediction refuted; conceptual successor (tablet/cloud) arrived 15 years late

metric_value: Larry Ellison and Michael Dell jointly predicted demise of Big Iron (high-end UNIX/mainframe) in favor of commodity x86 Linux clusters
notes: Dorin Aberdeen 2003: Ellison/Dell commodity server thesis; Oracle 10g and RAC as grid-on-commodity platform; directed against IBM pSeries/zSeries and HP Superdome

metric_value: Big Iron partially displaced by x86 but not eliminated; Oracle subsequently acquired Sun and sold Exadata engineered systems — the most expensive Big Iron in the market
notes: Oracle's own Exadata (2008) contradicted the commodity thesis; Exadata is engineered Big Iron at premium prices; IBM mainframe still shipping 2026; prediction partially right (UNIX displacement) but self-contradicted by Oracle's own product strategy

metric_value: ~10 observations 2009–2015 on Sun acquisition and integration
notes: THREAD-10: Sun Microsystems Acquisition. Oracle acquired Sun 2010 for $7.4B — acquiring Java/MySQL/Solaris/SPARC in a single transaction; most strategic technology acquisition in the archive

metric_value: Oracle acquired Sun to control Java — the most widely deployed enterprise application runtime — and to gain hardware systems business
notes: Kastner 2009 (2 obs): SPARC architecture on life support before Oracle acquisition; Oracle's rationale was Java control + vertical integration into hardware/software stack

metric_value: Oracle discontinued SPARC processor development 2017; Solaris development frozen 2018
notes: Oracle ended SPARC chip development with M8 processor 2017; Solaris 11.4 (2018) last major release; hardware business wound down; Java and MySQL the durable acquisitions

metric_value: Java remained the dominant enterprise programming language 15 years post-Oracle acquisition
notes: Java holds ~30% of enterprise application development share as of 2026 (RedMonk/Tiobe indexes); Oracle Java SE subscription model controversial but Java ecosystem intact; most durable asset from Sun acquisition

metric_value: MySQL remained world's most widely deployed open-source database 15 years post-Oracle acquisition
notes: MySQL holds dominant web/cloud application database position (WordPress/Meta/Twitter infrastructure); Oracle maintained community edition; MariaDB fork created by MySQL founders as hedge

metric_value: ~15 observations 2016–2026 on cloud pivot and OCI
notes: THREAD-11: Cloud Pivot and OCI Buildout. Oracle was among the last major enterprise software vendors to embrace cloud delivery; OCI Gen 2 (2016) launched as credible AWS/Azure alternative; Autonomous Database (2018) as primary differentiator

metric_value: Oracle OCI Gen 2 differentiated on security architecture (no shared tenancy for control plane) and price parity with AWS
notes: Oracle OCI Gen 2 claimed architectural superiority over AWS/Azure on isolation and security; aggressive pricing — 1/3 AWS price on comparable compute; designed to capture Oracle Database cloud migration

metric_value: Oracle Autonomous Database launched 2018 — first commercially available self-driving/self-patching/self-scaling database
notes: Autonomous DB positioned as the end of DBA manual operations; machine learning-driven; runs on Exadata cloud infrastructure; Oracle 23ai extended with AI vector search 2024

metric_value: Oracle OCI grew to approximately 4-5% public cloud market share by 2026 — small but profitable and growing
notes: OCI market share trails AWS (~33%) and Azure (~23%) and GCP (~12%) significantly; however Oracle claims OCI is growing faster than AWS in its comparable period; enterprise Oracle workloads represent core TAM

metric_value: Oracle Database 23ai introduced native AI vector search — completing the arc from Oracle InterOffice document summarization (1995) to in-database AI (2024)
notes: Oracle 23ai positions the database as the AI data platform; vector search on structured+unstructured data; in-database ML via Oracle Machine Learning; Select AI natural language query — all echoing InterOffice's 1995 document intelligence vision

metric_value: Oracle's core RDBMS franchise is the single most durable technology asset in the Kastner archive — surviving four decades of predicted displacement events with zero confirmed market exits
notes: Object-relational (refuted); NoSQL (refuted); cloud-native NewSQL (ongoing); Oracle Database has adapted to every architectural shift without losing enterprise market leadership

metric_value: Oracle's trajectory from InterOffice document summarization (1995) to Oracle 23ai vector search (2024) is the archive's most complete 'first hint to full realization' AI arc
notes: Kastner noted Oracle InterOffice as the first AI hint in the archive. Oracle 23ai closes the arc: the same company that offered proto-AI in a groupware product in 1995 now offers in-database generative AI in 2024

metric_value: Oracle Data Mart Suite for NT addressed mass-market data warehousing opportunity on Windows NT — first Oracle DW product targeting mid-market
notes: Aberdeen 1997 (14 obs): Oracle Data Mart Suite for NT hit mass-market sweet spot; pre-built data mart schemas; Oracle DB as foundation; positioned against Sagent / MicroStrategy on NT

metric_value: Oracle Analytics Cloud (2020) traces lineage from Data Mart Suite (1997) through OBIEE (2007) — 27-year business intelligence evolution
notes: Oracle Data Mart Suite → Oracle Discoverer → Oracle BI Enterprise Edition (Siebel Analytics) → OBIEE → Oracle Analytics Cloud; consistent BI investment across three decades

metric_value: Kastner 1993 RDBMS Report Card graded Oracle7 as market leader across performance / portability / SQL compliance / developer tools
notes: Kastner et al. 1993: Oracle7 received highest composite grade; IBM DB2 second; Sybase and Informix competitive on UNIX; Ingres weak; early benchmark for archive's most-analyzed technology category

metric_value: Aberdeen 2001: Point solutions vs. integrated Oracle Applications — ROI analysis favored integration for large enterprises
notes: Jones/Dwyer/Kastner Aberdeen 2001: Integrated Oracle Applications delivered measurable ROI through eliminated integration cost; point solution advantage eroded above 1000-employee threshold

metric_value: Oracle E-Business Suite supply chain positioned as real-time customer-requirement-driven planning platform
notes: Minahan Aberdeen 2000 (12 obs): Oracle SCM proposed real-time demand sensing + supplier collaboration via Internet; ahead of market adoption curve in 2000

metric_value: Oracle Exadata (2008) — Oracle's engineered Big Iron system — directly contradicted Larry Ellison's 2003 commodity-hardware predictions
notes: Ellison/Dell 2003: commodity x86 clusters will kill Big Iron. Oracle Exadata 2008: $500K–$2M engineered system combining proprietary storage cells with Oracle DB. The archive's clearest CEO self-contradiction

metric_value: Oracle Database and cloud services revenue approximately $20B annually as of FY2026
notes: Oracle FY2026 cloud and license revenue ~$20B+ for database-related products; Oracle total revenue ~$57B FY2026; database remains ~35% of revenue despite applications growth

metric_value: PL/SQL stored procedures remain Oracle's single most effective switching-cost mechanism — unchanged from Kastner's 1993 identification
notes: PL/SQL installed base represents hundreds of billions of lines of enterprise code globally; migration cost effectively locks Oracle DB customers; identified as strategic moat by Kastner 1993 and still operative 2026

metric_value: Oracle HCM Cloud competes with Workday for cloud HCM market; PeopleSoft acquisition (2005) provided the HCM capability foundation
notes: Oracle HCM Cloud vs. Workday is the defining cloud HCM contest as of 2026; Oracle's PeopleSoft-derived HCM capability the foundation; Workday growing faster in new-logo cloud HCM

metric_value: Oracle Cloud ERP (Fusion Financials) competes with SAP S/4HANA Cloud for large enterprise ERP cloud migrations
notes: Oracle Cloud ERP and SAP S/4HANA Cloud represent the two dominant enterprise ERP cloud choices as of 2026; Oracle stronger in financial services/utilities; SAP stronger in manufacturing

metric_value: Oracle InterOffice (1995) is the earliest product in the 73-study Kastner Oracle archive to offer an AI-adjacent feature (document summarization)
notes: No earlier study in the Oracle archive references document summarization or any automated intelligence extraction from text. This is the archive's proto-AI observation OBS-1.

metric_value: Oracle NCA defined a three-tier architecture: Oracle Web Application Server (app tier) + Oracle8 (data tier) + NC/browser (client tier)
notes: Aberdeen 1996: NCA coherently defined each tier; Ellison claimed this eliminated the Windows monopoly; architecture later validated as the web application model though Oracle's specific products did not win

metric_value: Oracle APEX (2004–present) is the durable successor to Developer/2000 — Oracle-native low-code development on Oracle DB
notes: Oracle APEX 24.1 (2024) is actively developed; dominates Oracle-native application development; ~10M APEX applications deployed globally; Developer/2000 lineage continues

metric_value: Oracle archive contains multiple confirmed prediction refutations — RDBMS displacement (2x refuted); NC device (refuted); Big Iron demise (partially refuted by Oracle itself)
notes: Unlike IBM (0 formal refutations) and Intel (9.7% refutation rate in viability rows) Oracle has a distinctive pattern: Ellison's competitive predictions about Oracle winning new markets frequently failed while Oracle's core franchise proved indestructible

metric_value: Oracle's paradox: the company that repeatedly predicted displacement of incumbents (PC, Big Iron, proprietary software) survived every prediction of its own displacement — while its own disruptive bets (NC, InterOffice) failed
notes: The Oracle archive documents a company whose external disruption predictions largely failed while its core franchise proved indestructible; Oracle is simultaneously the archive's most frequent predictor and most frequent self-refuter

Linux x86 emergence accelerated RISC/Unix deceleration. Prediction not confirmed.

metric_name: Actual outcome: NT impact on RISC/Unix for business-critical apps
metric_value: NT Server captured departmental/workgroup segment (shipments tripling 1995-1997) but Unix held enterprise OLTP and mission-critical deployments through 2000. NT 4.0 shipped April 1996 as predicted. Unix held ~717K server units in 1997 with 15% modest growth. Prediction confirmed for 1996-1998 period: NT complemented, did not displace RISC/Unix for business-critical production apps.
notes: Source: CNET NT server market grows (1998-01-27): 'NT experienced most growth in departmental servers serving 20-50 people.' Prediction confirmed.

metric_name: Actual outcome: Year-2000 mainframe replacement cycle opportunity
metric_value: Y2K drove significant server infrastructure investment 1998-2000. IBM pSeries Unix revenue grew 28% in 2000, 49% in Q4 2000 (IBM Annual Report 2000). However much Y2K spending was split across RISC/Unix, Windows NT, and emerging Linux x86 rather than purely benefiting RISC/Unix. The opportunity materialized but was shared across platforms.
notes: Source: IBM Annual Report 2000 (ibm.com). Y2K opportunity confirmed but RISC/Unix shared it with NT/Linux. Prediction partially confirmed.

metric_name: Actual outcome: Production Unix functionality advances (1996 agenda item 1)
metric_value: All major RISC/Unix vendors delivered significant production Unix improvements in 1996-1998: HP-UX 10.20 (1996) with improved POSIX; AIX 4.2 (1996) with 64-bit support; Solaris 2.6/7 (1997/1998) with large files and 64-bit; Digital Unix 4.0 with enhanced clustering. POSIX Single Specification v2 (1997) consolidated Unix standards. Prediction confirmed.
notes: Source: ACM Queue 64-bit article (2006); Unix Single Specification history. Production functionality advances delivered by all major vendors as prescribed.

metric_name: Actual outcome: 64-bit Unix transition (1996 agenda item 2)
metric_value: DEC Alpha was already 64-bit (since 1992). HP shipped PA-8000 64-bit processors in 1996 for HP-UX. Sun shipped UltraSPARC-II with Solaris 7 64-bit in 1998. IBM AIX 4.2 (1996) added 64-bit addressing. All major RISC/Unix vendors (except IBM being already in AS/400 64-bit path) transitioned to 64-bit within 12-18 months as predicted.
notes: Source: ACM Queue 'Long Road to 64 Bits' (2006); OpenPA.net HP PA-RISC PA-8000 history. Prediction confirmed with minor timing variation.

metric_name: Actual outcome: Workgroup interoperability advances (1996 agenda item 3)

metric_value: Telephone survey questionnaire — version 1 of RAMP quantitative instrument
notes: First version of the phone survey designed to collect structured quantitative data from approximately 70 enterprise respondents to validate MaXLine midline ATA disk market opportunity.

metric_value: Q1: Total disk available (GB or TB) — server-only; PC/workstations excluded
notes: Explicit exclusion of PC/workstation storage from Q1 reflects the enterprise-only focus of midline storage positioning. This server/enterprise vs. client distinction remained foundational in storage market sizing through the cloud era.

metric_value: Q2: Actual used storage (GB/TB); Q3: Maximum desired utilization (%)
notes: Measuring both actual utilization and maximum acceptable fill rate captures the over-provisioning gap — the excess capacity left as headroom. This delta was a key economic argument for midline storage: enterprises were paying for expensive FC disk capacity they couldn't fill past ~70%, while midline capacity could be used to higher percentages for cold data.

metric_value: Q4: Four-way split — internal DAS / external DAS / SAN / NAS — measured in GB/TB
notes: Four-way DAS/SAN/NAS breakout quantifies the installed base distribution. In 2003, DAS was still majority storage by capacity at many shops; SAN was growing in enterprise; NAS was growing in file. This breakout enabled market sizing of which architecture would be the deployment vehicle for midline ATA — answer proved to be both DAS refresh and SAN tiering.

metric_value: Q5: Expected storage growth in next 12 months (%)
notes: 12-month growth rate measurement. Enterprises in 2003 were experiencing 40-60% annual storage growth driven by email retention (Sarbanes-Oxley passed 2002), unstructured data explosion, and database growth. This growth rate was a market tailwind for midline storage: the cost of storing all that growth on FC disk was unsustainable.

metric_value: Q6: Storage mapped to OS — mainframe / Unix / Windows / Other (GB/TB per OS)
notes: OS-to-storage mapping enabled segmentation of midline storage market by platform. Windows servers proved to be the primary adoption vector for ATA/SATA midline storage (less conservative than Unix/mainframe shops), consistent with the hypothesis embedded in this question design.

metric_value: Q7: Seven redundancy methods probed — RAID 5 / RAID 1 / indexed snapshot / full-volume snapshot / remote mirroring / remote copy / tape generations
notes: Comprehensive seven-method redundancy taxonomy reveals the design assumption that enterprises mixed multiple protection methods. Importantly, the question lists BOTH disk-based protection (RAID/mirror/snapshot) AND tape-based backup — measuring the full protection stack that midline storage would need to integrate with.

metric_name: Snapshot count as a proxy for data value
metric_value: Q8: Number of on-disk copies (excluding parity RAID) plus tape copies — directly measures copy proliferation
notes: Measuring total copy count (disk + tape) reveals the hidden storage cost of data protection — a cost that midline storage could reduce if used as a less-expensive copy target. This proved prescient: purpose-built backup appliances (DataDomain, Quantum DXi) exploited exactly this dynamic.

metric_value: Q9: What percentage of online data does not need highest-availability storage? (closed transactions / old e-mail)
notes: This is the central market-sizing question: what fraction of expensive FC/SCSI disk was occupied by cold data that could move to midline? The answer from the survey reportedly showed 20-40% of enterprise disk was cold — directly sizing the midline TAM. This measurement methodology was replicated in every subsequent ILM and storage tiering market study.

metric_value: Q10: Would you accept (a) higher-capacity/slightly-less-performance or (b) same-size/similar-performance for cold data migration?
notes: Binary choice design tests the core MaXLine product hypothesis directly. Option (a) = MaXLine-style midline; option (b) = same-tier refresh. This simple binary was later refined into the 1-7 Likert scale in Survey v2, suggesting the binary wasn't discriminating enough.

metric_name: Disk capacity-speed gap as adoption context
metric_value: Q11: Despite capacity growing faster than speed, will you still move to larger capacity disks?
notes: This question establishes whether respondents understood the capacity/performance tradeoff and were already accepting it for general disk. If yes (as expected), it validates that the performance penalty of ATA was already being absorbed. This was a clever indirect test of ATA acceptability without mentioning ATA explicitly.

metric_value: Q12: Do you allow multiple applications to share an array?
notes: Shared array adoption was growing in 2003 as SAN matured. High shared-array adoption would mean midline storage could be deployed in shared arrays serving multiple cold-data workloads simultaneously, improving economics. Low adoption would mean per-application deployment.

metric_name: Disk technology installed base — three-way breakdown
metric_value: Q13: SCSI / FC / ATA percentage breakout with drive sizes and rotational speeds
notes: Three-way disk technology inventory (SCSI/FC/ATA). ATA percentage in 2003 enterprise environments was very low (<5% typically) — this question was designed to measure the baseline ATA penetration. Results would show near-zero ATA enterprise adoption, establishing the market as a greenfield opportunity for midline.

metric_value: Q14: Do you have performance bottlenecks? If yes: CPU / storage / network. If no: expect future bottleneck?
notes: Bottleneck identification serves dual purpose: (1) screens out sites where storage is NOT the bottleneck (ATA inappropriate); (2) sizes the population for whom storage performance is acceptable at midline levels. Storage bottleneck respondents are poor midline candidates; network/CPU bottleneck respondents are ideal.

metric_value: Q15-Q18: Formal SLA existence / informal criteria / consequences of unavailability and performance degradation
notes: SLA questions measure risk tolerance — respondents with strict formal SLAs for ALL applications are poor midline candidates; those with informal criteria or SLAs only for Tier 1 apps are ideal. This segmentation proved accurate: midline SATA succeeded first in shops with mixed-SLA environments.

metric_name: Backup window as structural pain point
metric_value: Q19-Q20: Backup window length (or online backup); specific issues — running out of window, job failure rate
notes: Backup window questions capture a secondary but important midline use case: if inactive data is migrated off primary arrays to midline, primary array backup windows shrink because less data must be backed up. This was a cost/operational benefit that proved important in actual MaXLine customer deployments.

metric_value: Q21: nearline storage / active archiving / mezzanine storage — tested for awareness
notes: Three-term awareness battery identical to interview guide. The inclusion in the telephone survey (vs. face-to-face) allows quantification of awareness rates across 70 respondents. Post-study, Aberdeen could report: X% of enterprises had heard of nearline, Y% of active archiving — market readiness metrics.

metric_value: Q22: Local / Regional / National / International / Global — five-level geographic scope
notes: Geographic scope demographic ensures survey captures global enterprises (most likely midline buyers) vs. local organizations. Global organizations managing multi-site storage had stronger economic justification for tiered storage to reduce replication costs across sites.

metric_value: Q23: CIO / CTO / IS Director-Manager / Technical Specialist / Hardware Engineer / Software Engineer / Programmer / Systems Analyst / DBA / Other
notes: Nine-category job title classification targets the actual storage purchase decision chain. CIO/CTO = budget approval; IS Director/Manager = RFP author; Technical Specialist/DBA = technical influencer. Targeting this full chain was methodologically correct for a capital storage purchase decision.

metric_value: Q25: Revenue from <$10M to >$5B in 9 bands
notes: Revenue banding enables segmentation of midline storage interest by company size. The hypothesis (confirmed in subsequent research) was that enterprises with >$1B revenue had the storage scale to justify midline tiering — smaller companies' storage volumes made the management complexity not worthwhile.

metric_value: Q26: IT budget from <$1M to >$500M in 9 bands
notes: IT budget classification directly sizes the storage purchase budget. Enterprises with IT budgets >$50M were the primary midline target; this question enabled filtering results to the addressable market. The budget bands were appropriate for 2003 enterprise storage spend patterns.

metric_value: Q27: CIO reports to CFO / President-CEO / Other
notes: CIO governance question quantifies the financial vs. strategic IT orientation. CFO-reporting CIOs (cost-focused) would be more receptive to midline storage's cost reduction story; CEO-reporting CIOs might prioritize capability. This segmentation was used to tailor the MaXLine value proposition.

metric_value: Q28: 25 industry verticals from Aerospace to Wholesale Trade
notes: 25-vertical industry classification enables identification of which verticals had the most acute midline storage need. Healthcare (HIPAA compliance data retention), Financial Services (trading records), and Manufacturing (CAD/CAM large files) proved to be the highest-adoption verticals for midline SATA storage — consistent with the workload classifications in the interview guide.

metric_value: SAN listed before NAS in architecture breakout — implicit ordering by enterprise primacy
notes: The ordering SAN before NAS in Q4 reflects the 2003 belief that SAN was the dominant enterprise future. SAN did dominate block storage; NAS grew faster than expected for file storage; both were eventually supplanted by hyperconverged infrastructure (HCI) and object storage. The prediction was partially correct.

metric_name: SAN vs. NAS growth trajectory outcome
metric_value: [UNVERIFIED]
notes: , SAN maintained dominance in Tier 1 block storage through 2015; NAS grew faster than expected for unstructured data; object storage (S3, Azure Blob) disrupted both for capacity tier by 2012. Midline SATA deployed in both SAN (EMC, HDS, IBM midline trays) and NAS (NetApp SATA) contexts.

metric_name: Remote copy as distinct from remote mirroring
metric_value: Q7(e) remote mirroring vs. Q7(f) remote copying — treated as distinct protection methods
notes: Distinguishing synchronous remote mirroring from asynchronous remote copy was technically correct in 2003. This distinction became the foundation of RPO/RTO SLA design and later cloud disaster recovery tiering (synchronous vs. asynchronous replication options in AWS/Azure DR services).

metric_value: Q24: Entire company / Subsidiary / Division / Department / Geographic BU / Other
notes: Scope of responsibility determines whether respondent's storage data represents enterprise-wide or unit-level figures — critical for accurate capacity sizing. This methodological care about scoping prevents double-counting and reflects Aberdeen's quantitative research rigor.

metric_name: Four small hockey sticks vs. one large — quarterly cycle advantages

metric_value: Flat booking/shipping curve works only if: (1) monopoly product; (2) demand greatly exceeds supply; (3) product life measured in years; (4) control of raw material supply; (5) labor surplus at low wages. These conditions are exceptions in high-tech.
notes: Casale uses 'pancake curve' as opposite of hockey stick; argues smooth operations are structurally impossible in competitive tech markets.

metric_name: Two methods to flatten the hockey stick
metric_value: Method 1 (Stick): Manage salesforce to optimize factory flow; goal is low-cost production. Method 2 (Carrot): Manage factory to maximize near-term sales; goal is market share leadership. Both are variants on the same theme.
notes: Casale's 'stick vs. carrot' framework for hockey-stick management prefigures S&OP (Sales and Operations Planning) thinking that became standard in the 1990s.

metric_name: Pitfalls of downsizing for backlog building (stick approach)
metric_value: Risks: (1) loss of market share as competitors deliver what you forego; (2) customer satisfaction slips if deliveries stretch; (3) newly announced competitive product can melt backlog and devalue WIP/finished goods inventories.
notes: Casale warns explicitly against 'the backlog trap' — excess backlog is 'a snare and delusion'. Cross-reference future EVP on backlog.

metric_name: GAAP-violation escalation ladder — cost-push dilemma responses
metric_value: Stage 1 (legitimate): Sales promotions, discounting, compensation adders. Stage 2 (legitimate): Borrowing sales from future periods via backlog. Stage 3 (legitimate): New product introductions, customer incentives, extended payment terms. Stage 4 (GAAP-violating): Cover the clock at quarter end. Stage 5: Book shipments where paperwork is questionable. Stage 6: Take contingency sales into revenue. Stage 7: Book as sales items not actually sold using intermediaries.

metric_value: VOS runs in every module; all modules equal; transparent local networking makes the federation appear as a single virtual computer to programs, programmers and users

notes: Anticipates modern location-transparent distributed file systems

metric_value: Single 125 nsec cycle-time high-speed bus implemented as two parallel buses with independent data and control-logic paths

Each board runs two parallel sets of logic; on output, results are compared; mismatch lights red LED, raises bus interrupt, takes board off-line; redundant partner continues; no other component is aware
notes: Foundational pair-and-spare implementation

metric_value: Single CPU board = 4 Motorola 68000s organized as 2 software-visible CPUs; redundant virtual/physical address-translation maps; redundant partner CPU board for board-level fault tolerance

notes: Cited by Kastner as the economic enabler: redundancy that 'was not practical until VLSI'

metric_value: Redundant config: N MB program-visible memory implemented as 2N MB physical, split across 2 controllers; 64K RAMs on 2MB boards; 375 nsec read cycle; 4-way interleaved; redundancy can be turned on/off dynamically
Each disk can have a duplicate on a separate controller; writes go to both; reads come from the disk that is not busy or whose heads are best positioned; read errors retried from mirror
notes: Effectively RAID-1 with optimization, predating Patterson/Gibson/Katz 1988 RAID paper

metric_value: Dual StrataLINKs run as parallel separate links; on failure of one, data are retransmitted over the survivor without affecting users

On hard failure, maintenance software process automatically calls the Stratus national service center and transmits a data packet with site and failure info; 'Stratus service people know within a minute of customer failures'
notes: Anticipates modern AIOps / IoT predictive-maintenance call-home telemetry

metric_value: A failed board can be replaced in a running system by a non-technical person without special tools and without affecting any user's program; VOS dynamically reconfigures
notes: Hot-swap modules in 1983 — well ahead of mainstream

metric_value: Application programs may be written in COBOL, PL/I, BASIC, FORTRAN or Pascal; all language features usable, including I/O statements

Single message queue can connect any number of servers with any number of requesters; queues redirect dynamically by changing the pathname to point to another module — applications scale without recompile
notes: Anticipates queue-based microservices and async messaging

metric_value: Phase I writes all updated records to disk and sets 'Phase I Commit' flag in file header; original disk image preserved; all involved nodes must report Phase I success before VOS authorizes Phase II commit; restart-salvage detects Phase I Commit flag
START / COMMIT / ABORT primitives in TPF; ABORT restores all files to pre-START state regardless of whether data is on a single processing module or distributed
System administrator can permit, permit-after-network-password, or deny incoming requests on each system node; access-control lists enforced across the network
Every file has an access-control list of (user-id, rights ∈ {execute, read, read/write}); per-user or per-group; no embedded passwords in programs; enforced regardless of access program/command

metric_value: Telephone survey questionnaire — version 2; refined and streamlined from v1
notes: Second version of the RAMP phone survey; Part One has 17 numbered questions (Q1-Q17 with some gaps) plus Part Two demographics. Key refinements: per-OS storage breakout replaces single total; 1-7 Likert scale replaces binary choice; terminology battery expanded from 3 to 5 terms.

metric_value: Q1: Which OSes does your organization use AND which are you directly responsible for? (Mainframe / Windows / Unix-Linux)
notes: V2 improvement: asking both organizational use AND personal responsibility screens for the authoritative respondent for each OS type. This ensures storage data for mainframe is provided by the mainframe team, not a Windows admin guessing. Methodological refinement over v1's single OS breakout question.

metric_name: Per-OS storage architecture breakout — v2 design
metric_value: Q4.1-Q4.3: Per-OS capacity share / DAS-SAN-NAS mix / 12-month growth / max fill rate — separately for mainframe / Windows / Unix
notes: Major v2 enhancement: breaking out storage architecture by OS (Q4.1 Mainframe / Q4.2 Windows / Q4.3 Unix/Linux) rather than asking for a single total. This reveals that mainframe, Windows, and Unix shops had dramatically different architecture mixes (mainframe=internal ESCON/FICON; Unix=SAN; Windows=DAS/NAS). This granularity was essential for product positioning.

metric_name: Windows and Unix/Linux treated as equivalents for open-systems storage
metric_value: Q4.2 and Q4.3 use identical structure; both excluded from mainframe category
notes: The parallel structure for Windows and Unix/Linux (with mainframe as a separate category) reflects the 2003 open-systems vs. proprietary divide. This was prescient: midline ATA storage adoption was almost entirely in the open-systems (Windows/Linux/Unix) category, consistent with the assumption embedded in Q4.

metric_name: Online disk vs. tape copy count
metric_value: Q5: Online disk copies (excluding original) / tape copies (each generation = one copy)
notes: Measuring total copy inventory (disk + tape) sizes the redundant storage overhead. If enterprises keep 2-3 tape generations plus 1-2 disk mirrors, the total redundant storage is 3-5x the original — midline storage as a copy target could cut cost of copies by 50-60%.

metric_name: Read-only / seldom-written data identification — refined framing
metric_value: Q6: Data that is effectively read-only or seldom written — closed transaction logs / old e-mail — but cannot yet be archived to tape
notes: V2 refines the cold-data concept from v1's "data that spins around" to "effectively read-only or seldom written." This more precise language maps directly to the data classification taxonomy that became standard in ILM: active (read/write) / reference (read-only) / archive (dormant). The Q6 category is the reference tier.

metric_value: Q7: What applications fall under the read-only/seldom-written category? (Open-ended)
notes: Open-ended application identification reveals which specific enterprise applications were generating cold data in 2003. Expected answers: closed ERP transaction logs, old email, completed project files, historical databases. The actual answers would identify the specific use cases that MaXLine should target in marketing.

metric_value: Q8: What percent of total storage is the read-only/seldom-written data?
notes: Quantitative market sizing: what percentage of existing enterprise storage is cold data suitable for midline? This number directly determines the addressable market for MaXLine. If 20-40% of enterprise storage is cold (as hypothesized). that justified significant midline investment.

metric_value: Q9: Rate willingness to trade off on 3 scenarios (1=unwilling to tradeoff; 7=sign me up today)
notes: KEY INSTRUMENT INNOVATION: v2 replaces v1's binary choice with a 1-7 Likert scale across three scenarios. Scale anchor at 7: "sign me up today" — a vivid buyer-intent anchor. This scale enables statistical segmentation: scores 5-7 = early adopters; 3-4 = fence-sitters; 1-2 = resisters. The Likert design was far more analytically powerful than v1's binary.

metric_name: Willingness scenario A — highest value proposition
metric_value: Q9(a): Higher capacity + slightly less performance + slightly less availability + ~50% cost reduction
notes: Scenario A is the MaXLine sweet spot: maximum capacity, significant cost savings (50%), modest performance and availability concessions. This is the most aggressive midline proposition. If enterprises score 5-7 here, midline is commercially viable. If they score 1-3, the availability concession is a dealbreaker — enterprise storage must be nearly perfect.

metric_name: Willingness scenario B — availability-reduced conservative case
metric_value: Q9(b): Current disk sizes + current performance + slightly less availability + ~30% cost reduction
notes: Scenario B tests whether the availability concession (not the capacity increase) is the key barrier. If B scores higher than A, enterprises want cost savings but won't accept larger/slower disks. If A scores higher than B, capacity increase is acceptable and performance/availability concession is the actual issue.

metric_name: Willingness scenario C — no tradeoff required
metric_value: Q9(c): Current disk size + current performance + current availability + ~30% cost reduction
notes: Scenario C is the ideal buyer dream: 30% cheaper with no concessions. If C scores dramatically higher than A or B, it reveals price sensitivity without tolerance for any tradeoff — indicating midline must be presented as functionally equivalent, not lower-spec. The delta between C and A/B measures the cost of the performance/availability concession.

metric_value: Q10: Has your current storage supplier discussed low-cost disk options with you? (Supplier name?)
notes: Competitive intelligence embedded in a market research question: identifies which vendors were already having the midline conversation with enterprise accounts. If major vendors (EMC, HP, IBM) were already engaging on low-cost disk, the market education was underway; if not, Maxtor/Aberdeen had an opportunity to lead the conversation.

metric_value: Q11: If yes [vendor discussed low-cost options] — plans to purchase in next 12 months (1=Not at all; 7=Already have)
notes: Second 1-7 scale measures purchase intent for low-cost storage already being discussed. Scale anchor 7 = "already have" measures installed base; 5-6 = pipeline; 3-4 = consideration. This is a classic sales funnel measurement instrument embedded in market research — directly maps to modern Net Promoter Score and buying intent surveys.

metric_value: Q12: How often do you restore one or more volumes from storage failure — weekly / monthly / quarterly / semi-annually / annually / less than annually
notes: Restore frequency measures storage reliability experience in practice. High restore frequency (weekly/monthly) indicates reliability is already a concern — these respondents may resist lower-availability midline. Low frequency (annually / rarely) indicates reliability is not a daily pain — these respondents are better midline candidates.

metric_name: Static data application identification — specific examples
metric_value: Q14: Single applications with very large non-volatile/static data — video data / images / data warehouse detailed / old e-mails
notes: Q14's explicit list (video / images / DW detailed data / old emails) is a remarkably accurate prediction of the primary midline storage use cases that proved commercially successful: medical imaging (PACS), video surveillance, data warehouse historical data, and email archiving were the four dominant midline ATA/SATA adoption categories by 2007-2010.

metric_name: Open-systems disk technology breakout — three types
metric_value: Q15: SCSI / FC / ATA percentage + drive sizes + rotational speeds — open-systems disk arrays only
notes: V2 scopes the disk technology question to open-systems only (Q15) — separate from mainframe (Q4.1). This is an important methodological refinement: mainframe disk (FICON-attached) was not relevant to midline positioning, and mixing it with open-systems data would have obscured the ATA baseline penetration.

metric_value: Q16: Five specific backup failure modes — offline window / job failure rate / cannot guarantee restore / management burden / restore time too long
notes: Five-symptom backup failure taxonomy captures the specific pain points that midline storage (as a backup target or as a destination for migrated cold data to reduce backup scope) could address. Each symptom maps to a midline benefit: (a) window = smaller backup set; (d) management burden = simplified tiered storage management; (e) restore time = SLA concern about midline restore speed.

metric_value: Q17: Active archiving / online archiving / mezzanine storage / nearline storage / low-cost storage — all five tested
notes: V2 expands from v1's 3-term to 5-term terminology battery, adding 'online archiving' and 'low-cost storage.' The addition of 'low-cost storage' as a plain-language alternative is revealing: if respondents knew 'low-cost storage' but not 'nearline,' it would indicate the concept resonated but the branding was missing. This was indeed the market reality — 'nearline' later won as the standard term.

metric_name: Midline storage as complementary vs. substitute tier
metric_value: Q9's three scenarios implicitly test whether midline is a substitute (Scenario C) or complement (Scenarios A/B) for existing storage
notes: The survey design encodes a critical strategic hypothesis: if customers score Scenario A (less performance + less availability) higher than C (same as today just cheaper), they are buying a DIFFERENT tier, not just a cheaper version of the same thing. This is the complement vs. substitute positioning question that determined Maxtor's go-to-market strategy.

metric_value: [UNVERIFIED]

metric_value: PCI-E: each lane 2.5GHz = 'x1'; up to x16 aggregated = 4 GB/s bandwidth. Divisible into scalable widths (e.g., x4 for InfiniBand/10GbE).

Key PCI-E attributes: (1) layered architecture; (2) RAS features — data integrity, advanced error logging via IPMI, hot-plug; (3) I/O consolidation/unification across buses; (4) advanced power/config management; (5) workstation graphics 2x AGP 8x; (6) virtual channels/isochrony/QoS for media I/O; (7) software compatible with PCI-X and PCI.

2004 PCI-E capabilities expected: serial graphics replacing AGP (4 GB/s over PCI-E, 2x AGP 8x); x8 links ~2x PCI-X 266; serial disk connections proliferating (SATA + SCSI); 10GbE served by PCI-E x8; InfiniBand at 4x freed from PCI-X bottleneck.

metric_value: Aberdeen approached 28 companies; 5 agreed to participate (Dell, IBM, Unisys, Computer Associates, Xerox). Most companies treat launch process as strategic and confidential.
All 5 companies described a global, standardized launch process across hardware/software/services product groups.
2 companies said variations are insignificant; 3 acknowledged individual product groups had some autonomy with meaningful product-to-product variation.

Launch execution always involves a matrix-managed cross-functional team led by a launch team owner, integrating product dev, test, procurement, manufacturing, marketing, sales channel, fulfillment, training, support, finance, AR, PR.
2 of 5 companies had separate launch organizations reporting into VP Marketing (Product and Solutions Launch; Product Release Strategy). 3 had no common launch organization.
Lead time — End of product beta testing: 14 days before launch (Appendix A-1); 15-30 days (A-2). Often data is collected all the way to launch decision.
Product Configurator Ready: requirements 30-45 days; implemented 7-14 days. Order systems require data 45 days in advance; lead time rarely met.
Launch Readiness Review: often starts 90 days before launch, final readiness review 7-14 days prior, senior-management Time-to-Market decision meeting 1-7 days prior.
Pricing (U.S.) signoff: guidelines required 60 days prior; signoff 30-45 days prior. Lead times often not met (may be <30 days).
Product literature print run complete: 14 days (often not until launch date). Catalog placements 30 days. 3-4 weeks out to last-minute.
Press and analyst materials: briefings 45 days prior; materials sent 5 days prior or at launch. Press 2 weeks; analysts 4-6 weeks (separate respondent).
Training Materials: 14 days (one respondent) to 4-6 weeks (another).
Web site: 30 days before launch (multiple respondents agreed).
Sales training: 30 days prior. BOM: 60-90 days prior.

Seven delivery methods used across respondents: (1) hardcopy, (2) Web e-learning, (3) Web site, (4) classroom, (5) electronic documents (.pdf), (6) intranet database, (7) collaboration software. Trend toward webinars.

While a rigorous published framework is defined for the organization, it is rarely executed precisely in an identical fashion — difficult to differentiate between process as defined and as implemented.
As timeframes tighten and pressures for new products increase, there is increasing variation from standard process and increasing autonomy of individual product groups/business units.
In companies without a separate launch org, process-change authority is vague — senior executives of product groups approve changes but no clear owner.
At least one respondent (implied IBM) uses Lotus Notes collaboration software throughout much of the launch process.
Work is done differently across regions; globalization/internationalization typically first North America then rolled out and translated locally; 30 days for sales-literature translation.

Age twelve; described as 'Basic Business Controls 101, delivered at age twelve.'

Adding machines, pencils, and lined accounting workbooks — no path to making the job faster or smarter.

metric_value: Every single check was touched by human hands at minimum half a dozen times before being returned to account holder.
Making an airline reservation required a half-hour telephone call and a trip to the travel agent to collect a physical ticket.
Commerce was extraordinarily labor intensive, and almost nobody in 1960 thought there was anything unusual about that.
Enrolled at Cornell's School of Hotel Administration in 1965 expecting to find automation answers there.
First Friday concert: The Beach Boys; second: The Rolling Stones; fourth: Bob Dylan.

metric_name: Hotel Ezra Cornell punch-card automation attempt
metric_value: Upper-class accounting team used donated IBM punch-card tabulating equipment to automate Hotel Ezra Cornell (HEC) weekend books.
Programmed by physical wiring on a plugboard — patching cables like an old telephone switchboard — not software.
Could sort, count, and add 80-column card data but could not perform conditional logic (if-then category assignment) with sufficient flexibility via plugboard wiring.
'Our eyes were bigger than what the technology could deliver.' Team conceded defeat; fell back on paper receipts and human bookkeepers.

metric_name: Decision to take a year off and join MIT
metric_value: Took a year off from Cornell; took a job at MIT as a full-time computer operator to learn computing at the foundation level.
Reader-printer workhorse: ingested punch-card batches, wrote to magnetic tape at 800 bpi, printed mainframe output. 'The loading dock.'
Daytime: timesharing for dozens of simultaneous academic users. Off-peak: batch mode processing jobs queued on tape.
Techniques developed at MIT on the 7094 fed directly into the Multics operating system.
Dedicated development machine with attached graphics workstation and trackball — 'an exotic luxury in 1966.'

metric_name: Longevity of climate code on IBM 360/65
metric_value: Base FORTRAN airflow-analysis code written on the MIT 360/65 was still embedded in climate models as late as the 2020s.

metric_name: Batch processing economic model of 1960s computing
metric_value: Three-machine pipeline (cards in, tape to mainframe, results back) defined the economics of computing for the next decade.
Noisy rooms, constant pressure to keep jobs moving, modest pay — 'factory work in a white coat.'
Taught himself FORTRAN on the company's idle overnight CPU cycles — 'on the company dime.'
Taught himself IBM assembler during quiet overnight hours on the operator's own accounts.
Spacewar! video game appeared permanently installed on the 360/65 graphics workstation; Kastner could play it on a '$5 million mainframe' during overnight shifts.
Helped a cryptic researcher run classified simulations. Researcher said only: 'Things that go boom.'
Developing foundations of timesharing and multiuser computing that would eventually produce the Multics operating system.
Researchers argued about artificial intelligence 'with a fervor that felt more like religion than engineering.'

metric_name: Thesis: client-server as permanent architectural principle
metric_value: Client-server was not a temporary fad; separating presentation, business logic, and data management was correct system design. Technologies would change but logical separation persisted.
Relational databases had won the data management battle. ACID transaction guarantees + SQL flexibility = universal standard for operational systems.
Personal mission from 1985 to 1995 was championing the RDBMS that could handle both transactions AND query/reporting — the killer combination.
Proprietary platforms were economically doomed. Cost advantages of standardized components at volume were overwhelming. Strategic implication: architect for platform replaceability.
Aberdeen hired a Linux analyst as soon as Red Hat took off, reflecting the firm’s open-architecture conviction.

Data becoming a strategic asset, not merely an operational record. Enterprises analyzing customer behavior/market trends faster than competitors had sustainable advantages. Kastner has a circa-1991 slide of today’s AI-driven analysis model.

As client-server proliferated, integration complexity exploded into N-squared complexity. Pattern: architectural proliferation → integration pain → demand for integration platforms → new standards → further proliferation.

S-N-R: road map for integrating heterogeneous computer systems. Systems-of-record at center; middle manager rings run productivity apps on peer-peer networks; productivity nodes on LAN. ‘Lego for building systems architectures.’
Proprietary platforms doomed; Unix and x86 to dominate. Outcome: correct on direction but Unix fragmentation persisted; Linux won via open licensing not technical standardization.

metric_name: Arguments against VC: culture and control
metric_value: VC meant governance changes, growth imperatives, and pressure to build revenue ahead of profitability. Cooperative partnership model difficult to maintain at larger scale with institutional investors.

Aberdeen partnership model 1990–1997 (7 years) validated principles for building specialized research/advisory firms in emerging technology markets.

metric_name: Lesson: specialization scales better than generalization
metric_value: Deep domain expertise created more defensible value than broad market coverage; clients paid premium rates for analysts with true technical depth.
Multi-layer revenue sharing was complex to administer but essential for maintaining firm cohesion; partners had strong incentives to collaborate rather than compete internally.

metric_name: Lesson: risk-reward on hiring aligns incentives
metric_value: Making hiring partners responsible for analyst productivity ensured careful decisions and effective deployment; 35% margin reward made risk worthwhile.

metric_name: Lesson: publishing generates better leads than cold calling
metric_value: Free research distribution built trust and demonstrated expertise before sales conversation. Prospects who consumed research were easier to close and more satisfied clients.

metric_name: Lesson: technical credibility opens different doors
metric_value: Analyst depth in technical domains created opportunities with engineering organizations and technical executives that market analysis alone couldn’t access. Analysts could often install and configure products they covered.

metric_name: Lesson: culture formation happens early and persists
metric_value: Cooperative, technically deep, publishing-centric culture established in first few years shaped Aberdeen’s identity even as the firm scaled and changed ownership.

metric_name: Partnership synergy: whole greater than parts
metric_value: Partners could charge more, be trusted more, and accomplish more collectively than any could have done alone. ‘The whole was genuinely greater than the sum of its parts. That is the hardest thing to build and the easiest thing to destroy.’

metric_name: Pattern 1: Economic winner displaces technical winner
metric_value: Every major platform transition was driven primarily by economics, not superior engineering. Technical superiority is necessary but not sufficient; technical adequacy plus economic advantage is the sufficient condition.
notes: Named pattern; one of seven recurring structural dynamics Kastner considers most reliable.

metric_value: Mainframe was not technically obsolete when minicomputers displaced it; it was economically uncompetitive for departmental workloads.
Minicomputer was not technically obsolete when x86 servers displaced it; it was economically uncompetitive compared to commodity hardware manufactured at scale.
Unix was not technically inferior to Linux; Linux won on licensing economics and community development.

metric_name: Pattern 2: Proprietary platforms fund their own replacement
metric_value: Proprietary platform achieves leadership through innovation, captures high margins, which attract commodity-based open alternatives that improve rapidly and displace the proprietary platform.
notes: Named pattern; described as 'consistent across every cycle I observed.'

metric_value: IBM funded the research that produced Unix, exemplifying Pattern 2 where proprietary platform margins fund the open alternative that displaces them.

metric_value: "The best way to get valid performance measures is to use a widely recognized, easily understood, and easily duplicated benchmark in which time, cost, throughput, and recovery are clearly specified."
notes: claim: Benchmark selection rationale: DEC consulted industry analysts on what to measure and received unanimous advice to use a widely recognized, easily duplicated benchmark with clearly specified time, cost, throughput, and recovery requirements. DEC chose the industry-standard Debit-Credit benchmark.

metric_name: Debit-Credit benchmark spec as stated by Glorioso
metric_value: "95% of these transactions must be completed in one second or less. Cost per transaction is calculated by a formula which divides the five-year cost of hardware, software, and maintenance exclusive of staff by the number of transactions per second."
notes: claim: Debit-Credit benchmark spec as stated by Glorioso: one TPS = 100 tellers, 10 branches, one transaction per 100 seconds. 95th-percentile response time ≤ 1 second. Cost = 5-year hardware + software + maintenance exclusive of staff, divided by TPS.

metric_value: Methodology factor 1: CPU speed and cache size; faster chip with greater cache wins within architecture; Pentium 4 at 1.8 GHz beats Celeron at 1.8 GHz due to greater cache
notes: Kastner CPU valuation criterion

metric_value: Methodology factor 2: memory size and speed; 128MB significantly slower than 256MB; multimedia users want 512MB; DDR faster than SDRAM; RDRAM best for high-end Pentium 4s
notes: Kastner memory valuation criterion

metric_value: Methodology factor 3: integrated 56K modem and 10/100 Ethernet should be standard; no need to use expansion slots for these functions
notes: Kastner modem/NIC valuation criterion

metric_value: Methodology factor 4: hard drive: 7200 RPM faster than 5400 RPM and preferred; 40GB entry-level adequate; 80GB satisfies most; multimedia archivists may want more
notes: Kastner HDD valuation criterion

metric_value: Methodology factor 5: 17" monitors under $100 in bundles; 19" upgrade provides 40% more pixel real estate; 19" flat-panel monitor is to die for; retail bundle deals often include monitor and printer
notes: Kastner monitor valuation criterion

metric_value: Methodology factor 6: Windows XP Home adequate for most home users; XP Pro more valuable for power users, home office, and small business
notes: Kastner OS valuation criterion

metric_value: Methodology factor 7: creditable color printers at $50 and up; often bundled with PC and monitor to maximize margin while creating ink/paper customer; no one should buy a PC just for the printer
notes: Kastner printer valuation criterion

metric_value: Methodology factor 8: software bundle; CD-burner enabling software vs. productivity software like Microsoft Office; latter helps PC function as office PC
notes: Kastner software bundle valuation criterion
